summary: Describes Path MTU Discovery for IPv6, largely derived from the IPv4 version in RFC 1191. It lets a sender find the largest packet size that fits the whole path. It replaces RFC 1981.

eli5.summary: Before moving a big couch, you check the narrowest door along the way. This lets a computer find the biggest packet that fits.

questions: what is an icmpv6 packet too big message
why is icmpv6 blocking a problem for pmtud
subtitle: How an IPv6 sender learns the biggest packet that fits every link on the way to the destination.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 sender wants to use the largest packets that can cross the whole path without fragmentation, but it only knows the size limit of its own first link.
tldr.mechanism: The sender starts by assuming the first hop's MTU. Any node that cannot forward a packet drops it and returns an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message carrying the MTU of the constricting link, and the sender lowers its estimate to match.
tldr.outcome: Nodes avoid wasting capacity on tiny packets and avoid IPv6 fragmentation, but the scheme breaks down when ICMPv6 messages are blocked, which is why RFC 4821 offers a fallback. This document obsoletes RFC 1981.

facts.label: Earliest increase probe
facts.value: 5 minutes after a Packet Too Big message

today: RFC 8201 is an Internet Standard and is not itself obsoleted or updated. It replaces RFC 1981 as the definition of Path MTU Discovery for IPv6.

sections.title: Why Packet Size Needs Discovering
sections.content:
An IPv6 node with lots of data sends it as a series of packets. Each packet should be no larger than the Path MTU (PMTU), which is the minimum link MTU of all the links in the path. Larger packets can be fragmented, but the RFC says it is usually preferable to use the largest size that crosses the path without IPv6 fragmentation.

Implementing the mechanism is optional: IPv6 nodes should implement it, and a minimal implementation (the RFC mentions a boot ROM) may omit it. Nodes that skip it must use the IPv6 minimum link MTU from RFC 8200 as their maximum packet size. That works, but it usually means smaller packets than necessary and suboptimal throughput.

The RFC also warns about a failure mode. If ICMPv6 messages are blocked, a connection can complete the TCP three-way handshake and then hang when data flows. This state is called a black-hole connection.
sections.eli5: Every road has a narrowest spot. If you only ever drive tiny cars, you waste trips. If you drive a huge truck, it may get stuck. This RFC is how you find out the biggest truck that fits.

sections.title: The Basic Idea
sections.content:
The source node first assumes the PMTU is the known MTU of the first hop. If a packet is too large for some node on the path, that node discards it and sends back an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message. The source then lowers its assumed PMTU to the MTU of the constricting hop reported in that message.

Discovery ends when the estimate is less than or equal to the actual PMTU. Several rounds may be needed, because a link with a smaller MTU may sit further along the path. A node may also choose to stop early by sending nothing larger than the IPv6 minimum link MTU.

Paths change over time. Decreases show up through Packet Too Big messages. To notice increases, a node periodically tries a larger size, which will almost always get a packet dropped, so this should be done infrequently.

The mechanism also works for multicast: one packet can trigger several Packet Too Big messages, and the minimum PMTU across the paths in use sets the size of later packets. Discovery is needed even for a destination that appears to be on the same link, because a neighboring router acting as a proxy can make a distant node look local.
sections.eli5: You guess the first door is the narrowest. If a bouncer further on says "too big, only this wide," you remember that and use smaller boxes next time.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Do
sections.content:
The rules apply only to nodes that implement the mechanism. This document uses lowercase "must" and "should" and does not cite RFC 2119, because it updates a document written before RFC 2119 existed.

  • Nodes should check that the payload of a Packet Too Big message matches traffic they actually sent.
  • A message reporting a next-hop MTU below the IPv6 minimum link MTU must be discarded, and a node must not reduce its estimate below that minimum.
  • On a valid message the node must reduce its PMTU estimate and the size of packets it sends along the path, and must detect decreases as fast as possible.
  • A node must never raise its estimate because of a Packet Too Big message.

Increases may be probed, but not sooner than 5 minutes after a Packet Too Big message was received for that path. The recommended timer is twice the minimum, 10 minutes.

The ban on raising the estimate from a message exists because such a message could be stale, forged in a denial-of-service attack, or a result of multiple paths with different PMTUs.
sections.eli5: If someone shouts "the door is narrower!" you believe them and shrink your box. But if someone shouts "the door is wider!", you do not believe it, and you try carefully later, not too often.

sections.title: Implementation Notes: Layering and Caching
sections.content:
Section 5 is advice for implementers, not a specification. It suggests that the IP layer store PMTU information and the ICMPv6 layer process Packet Too Big messages, so each packetization layer (a transport such as TCP, or a protocol built on UDP) does not have to redo the work. Layers learn of changes through the maximum send transport-message size, MMS_S, which is the largest sendable IP packet (EMTU_S) minus the IPv6 header and extension headers.

The node must associate a PMTU with some local representation of a path, and the implementation chooses which. The options discussed are one value for the whole node, one per destination address, or one per flow id when flows are in use. For nodes with multiple interfaces, PMTU information should be kept for each IPv6 link. Initially the value is the first-link MTU, and a tentative value from a Packet Too Big message replaces it only if it is smaller.

Cached values can go stale. Too-large values are caught almost at once, but nothing reveals a too-small value, so implementations should age cached values and, after about 10 minutes without a decrease, probe for a larger PMTU. Implementations should also let the timeout be changed, even to infinity.
sections.eli5: The post office keeps a note of the narrowest door for each street, and tells every delivery person who uses that street. It also throws away old notes after a while, in case the street got wider.

sections.title: What Transports Do When a Packet Is Dropped
sections.content:
A packetization layer such as TCP must use the PMTU for the path and should not send segments that produce larger packets, except to probe, and a probe must not be fragmented to the PMTU. A TCP implementation must also respect the MSS value received from its peer, which reflects the receiver's reassembly limit (EMTU_R). The MSS option it sends is independent of the PMTU.

A Packet Too Big message means a packet was dropped, and a reliable upper layer recovers through its normal retransmission. The retransmission may instead be triggered at once by the notification, but only for the connection named in the message, and it should be no larger than the new PMTU. Because there may be smaller limits further along, a layer that retransmits is also responsible for congestion control of its retransmissions. A loss caused by a PMTU probe and signalled by a Packet Too Big message must not be treated as a congestion notification.

Transports that cannot repacketize on retransmission may let the IP layer fragment the original segment. The RFC also notes an update on NFS, which now must run over a standardized transport that avoids congestion.
sections.eli5: When a box gets bounced, the sender packs it into smaller boxes and tries again, but does not panic as if the whole road were jammed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism allows two denial-of-service attacks, both based on forged Packet Too Big messages. In the first, the false message claims a much smaller PMTU. Because a node never sets its estimate below the IPv6 minimum link MTU, a victim only suffers suboptimal performance. In the second, the false message claims a larger PMTU than reality, which could briefly block the victim. Because a node must not raise its estimate based on such a message, it should not be vulnerable.

Both can cause a black-hole connection. If ICMPv6 filtering stops legitimate Packet Too Big messages from arriving, the source never learns the real PMTU. Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (RFC 4821) does not rely on ICMPv6 and is considered more robust, and RFC 4890 gives recommendations for filtering ICMPv6. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A prankster might shout fake door-size warnings. The rules say you never go below the smallest safe size and never trust a "bigger door" shout, so pranks only cost a little.

sections.title: Relation to Earlier Documents
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 1981, which was itself based largely on RFC 1191 for IPv4. Several IPv4 parts were not needed: router behavior is defined in ICMPv6, there is no Don't Fragment bit in IPv6, TCP MSS selection is covered in RFC 8200, and old-style messages and MTU plateau tables are unnecessary because every Packet Too Big message reports the MTU of the constricting link.

Changes since RFC 1981 include clarifying that the purpose is to reduce the need for IPv6 fragmentation, adding text on blocked ICMPv6 and a short summary of PLPMTUD, adding validation of Packet Too Big payloads, storing PMTU per link on multi-interface nodes, removing text on Routing Header type 0, generalizing the TCP section to all packetization layers, and updating the NFS text.
sections.eli5: This is a cleaned-up new edition of an older rulebook, with the outdated parts removed and the lessons from blocked messages added.

messages.label: ICMPv6 Packet Too Big
messages.note: Carries the MTU of the constricting link; the packet is dropped.

messages.label: Smaller packet
messages.note: Estimate lowered, never below the IPv6 minimum link MTU.

viz.caption: KEY RULES FOR PACKET TOO BIG HANDLING

items.title: Validate
items.text: Check that the message answers traffic actually sent.

items.title: Floor
items.text: Discard reports below the IPv6 minimum link MTU.

items.title: Decrease fast
items.text: Lower the PMTU estimate as soon as a valid message arrives.

items.title: Never raise
items.text: Do not increase the estimate based on a message.

items.title: Probe slowly
items.text: No increase probe within 5 minutes; 10 minutes recommended.
